Every change tried this session moves 'alive at 5,000 frames' (96 seeds, fixed budget) inside 54–68 of 96 and the pop rate inside 2.4–2.8 rows per 1,000 frames: share bound on the line search, a resumable reach search, room for the telegraph's block when raising, a guide that also reads a match across the row, hollow ×2, spend ×2, raise room +2/+4, clearing earlier (3 and 5 rows from the top), stalls started earlier. Two of them (the row guide, keying kept searches on the board they start from) scored clearly worse and were undone.

Break-finding is not what limits survival. A bot given unlimited work on the break search (an oracle, 46 seeds) survived the same as the shipped one: 33, 30 and 32 alive at 5,000 frames for oracle, current and older builds; it pops only 11% more rows (2.76 against 2.49 per 1,000 frames).

Deaths come from a standing pile, not a burst: in the 24 deaths of one scan, 15 had 8 or more rows of garbage on the board 1,000 frames before, 0–12 cells landed in the last 400 frames, and the board held 15–47 panels. Fatal landings are 20% of landings under 30 panels and 3% above.

The pile is a block taller than the board: rows pop one at a time (6 cells, ~42 frames, the next row needs its own match), each pop turns a row of garbage into a row of panels, so a pop alone does not lower the stack plus pile; only matches do. The bot lives topped, on stop time from chains, for long stretches.

Where the cycle time goes: between two pops (median 280 frames, shortest 71) 43% of frames are holds and 26% are a break line waiting for its pair to settle; the engine itself needs ~80 frames from the press to the pop. Holds with a break in reach fell from 47 of 60 to 11 of 60 when the kept searches stopped restarting on every pop frame.

Think budget: 0.37 per 1,000 frames over 8 ms on the fixed scan with the cheaper guide (5.85 with the first, dearer guide, which is why it was calibrated before going on). Input budget: 0 frames over.

Search clock: a step now waits for every pair still moving -- the root board's settle times (every pair, not only swappable ones) and each earlier step of its line, a clear's settle being its flash, face and pops. Lines the search accepted were priced 36-54 frames and pressed 106-255 by the engine; now priced within 0-5 frames of the engine's presses (24-seed scan, commit 4aa4d3a41a: mean 9,279 against 8,928 for its predecessor, one seed alive, input clean).

The search-clock commit raised frames over the think budget on the FIXED scan (no wall-clock guard) to 2.1-3.0 per 1,000 against 0.6-0.8 before (same seeds, repeated scans): the search costs about 7% more per unit of work (0.097 -> 0.104 ms/kwork on seed 12), and the over-8 ms decisions are all at full work with 0.15 ms/kwork, so a few percent on the mean moves the tail threefold. The ordinary scan, which tells the bot the time, reads 0.26 per 1,000 (48 frames in 181,157), under the line.
Reading logs: train.lua's F lines and 'died F' are FRAMES; every bot log line (clock, PRESS, PLAN, ARBOPTS) is the game CLOCK, which is frame + 189. A death at frame 558 is clock 747.

The mode: TrainingMenu sends 50 slabs of 6x12 a volley, 900 frames between volleys, so the supply never runs out; with a 12-row slab any rest position puts garbage in row 12, so the board is topped for the whole game and survival is never missing a cycle. A break flashes the whole block for 38 + 7 x (3 + its cells) frames (preStopTime 143-458 observed, 350-600 frames a break) and then converts one row; stop time earned meanwhile is held until the flash ends (preStopTime counts down first).

24 seeds, local, fixed budget, 12,000 frames: 779 flash ends, 28 followed by a death. Stop time banked at the flash's end: under 30 frames in 29% of flash ends and 18 of the 28 deaths (7% of such flash ends die); 30 or more in 71% and 10 deaths (about 1.6%). Frames to the next break after a flash end: median 60-75 whatever the stop, p90 about 250. A banked stop of 60-90 (a combo of four or more fired during the flash) is the one measured lever on survival.

Tried against that, 24 seeds at 12,000 frames (baseline 9 alive, mean 7,837): a combo that digs under the pile counts as cash when the topped board holds under 30 frames of stop -> 5 alive, mean 6,832; four times the reach search's work -> 4 alive, mean 5,893. Both undone.

What a dying board looks like (seed 10, frame 1,664 of 2,138): five rows of panels under nine rows of garbage; in the 280 idle searches of the next 700 frames no combo or chain was reachable once. Material, not timing, is short: a break spends three panels and the conversion returns six, a plain clear spends three and returns none, and nothing rises while topped. 30,000 frames means about 70 flash cycles a seed with a miss chance under 0.1% each; the measured chance is about 3.5% a flash end.

The end of a flash is the whole game. With the garbage block above row 12 its conversion gives no rise lock (pa.c updateActivePanelCount counts rows up to the board's height), so a board with no stop banked dies about 9 frames after the flash ends (seed 7: pre 0 at clock 10139, dead at 10148). A break line needs the converted row's colours, which show only then, and a walk of a few cells; nothing can be pressed in 9 frames unless the cursor is already there and the line is one swap.

Bridging that gap with swaps is closed by the game: wiggleCanSwap (pa.c) charges health when the same two panels are swapped again at the same cursor cell while the board is topped with no stop, pre-stop or shake and no other panel moving. A swap locks the rise for 5 frames and cannot be pressed again sooner, so the pair under the cursor cannot be swapped back; a different pair needs a cursor move (4+ frames) and leaves a hole. A bridge option on the engine judge confirmed it: a chain of twelve swaps bought 6-7 frames, not 60.

A search that finds breaks the decision does not: the probe (unbounded soonest-first search, then the judge) found a live break in a hold decision on 9 of 26 probes of seed 17's last 200 frames and none on most others, once lines the judge rejects are not counted. Such a line needed 480,000 work against the decision's 56,000, and it is open only for the first ~13 frames of a flash; a persistent soonest-first search beside the guided one (slot 4) fixed seeds 9, 18 and 22 and lost seeds 16 and 5, mean 7,955 against 7,837 at 12,000 frames: undone.

Where a flash end is fatal (24 seeds, local, fixed budget, 12,000 frames, 812 flash ends, 15 deaths): stop time banked at the flash end 0 frames -> 11 of 150 fatal (7.3%), 1-29 -> 2 of 96, 30-59 -> 1 of 94, 60 or more -> 1 of 472 (0.2%). Panels on the board at the flash end: under 20 -> 6 of 65 (9.2%), 20-23 -> 3.2%, 24-27 -> 1.6%, 28 and over -> 0.3%. A topped combo gives 60 frames of stop whatever its size from 4 to 8, a chain 88 + 2 per link past the first (90, 92, 94, 98); a break itself gave a combo or a chain in none of 470 probes.

Not the lever (each 24 seeds, 12,000 frames, local, fixed budget; baseline 15 deaths, 12,539 frames a death): four times the work and 16 times the search storage 20 deaths (the 4,096-line / 12,288-board tables made 65,536 / 786,432 for the kept searches); no input limit 18 deaths; no downtime attack 15; no lineup that clears 17; survival ranked before readiness 16; the scramble offered even when a plain clear lives longer 21; a combo that digs counted as cash on a topped board 21 (stop 0 at 13% of flash ends, down from 18%, but 24.9 panels at the flash end against 29.5). Search power does not buy survival here: material and stop time do, and they cost each other. Nothing from this is in the code.

Search found breaks the decision did not: with the larger storage, a probe over the last 250 frames before four deaths found a live break of 4 to 9 swaps in 14 of 18, 4 of 22, 7 of 22 and 8 of 16 windows, at 150,000 to 2,000,000 work against the decision's 56,000. A break of five swaps is 48 to 70 frames of presses; the decisions that ended in death held for the frames in between.

Seed 3 died at frame 532, the earliest of the scan: a six-wide block perched on two columns seven panels high with the other four columns hollow beneath it. The only contact with the garbage was the top of those two columns, no break was within six swaps (guide 5.14 of 6.14), a plain clear bought 39 frames and the board died nine frames after it ended with 31 panels on it.

The same build on fresh seeds: 25 to 48 (local, fixed budget, 12,000 frames) gives 15 deaths and 9 alive, one death per 13,330 frames, against 15 and 9 (12,539) on seeds 1 to 24. The rate is not a fit to the seeds the code was tuned on.

Fatal flash ends split by what flashed (24 seeds, 815 flash ends, 15 fatal): after a clear's pop with no stop banked 7 of 73 (9.6%); after a break's flash with no stop 4 of 78 (5.1%); after a break's flash with 1-59 banked 3 of 133; with 60 or more banked 1 of 473. The largest class is a plain clear bought to hold a topped board whose pop ends with nothing prepared behind it.

A lookahead on the engine (the board a break leaves, once its garbage has converted and nothing is in the air, played by lineConverted; the next break or clear looked for on it in the time nb_drain_in says it has): 4 to 9 percent of chosen breaks were followed by a break that fits, and one swap pressed during the flash made one fit in 7 of 14 flashes that had none. Wired into the arbiter as a ranking key and as preparation swaps it was worse, 18 to 21 deaths a 24 seeds against 15 (seeds 25-48: 18 against 15); with the follow-up allowed to be any clear, 24 of 24 died, mean life 3,802. The follow-up that fits is mostly a clear that spends panels, and spending panels is what the starved boards die of. Not in the code.

Lookahead run with its work free of the decision's budget (so it takes nothing from the other stages): 24 of 24 dead, mean 5,245. The idea, not the budget, is what loses. A break search rooted on the board the running break leaves (lineConverted), persisted by that board across the flash's frames, gave 14 deaths a 24 seeds on seeds 1-24 and 16 on 25-48, against 15 and 15: neutral, not kept. Switching the opening raise off: 18 deaths.

In the last 300 frames before eight deaths, an unbounded search (500 frames of time, 300,000-480,000 work) found a break in 1, 4, 9, 7, 7 and 5 probes of seeds 1, 2, 3, 15, 5 and 9 but pressed after the board loses health: seed 1 by exactly 10 frames in each of nine probes, seed 2 by 7 to 17, seed 15 by 8 to 25, seed 3 by 9. Seed 9 had a break in time in 24 of 26. The deaths are not for lack of a break anywhere on the board but a handful of frames of protection, and a plain clear holds a topped board for about 72.

Chain from the converted row, the owner's board (seed 1, frame 5,001): the converted panels fall on the pile and one that completes a match there is a chain link (stop 88 + 2 a link topped). A search of every swap and pair of swaps pressed during the flash, each played on the engine to the board at rest (lineAfterBreak) and scored by the frame that board loses health left alone, finds them: the best prep gains +20 to +65 frames over the hold, and a prep that predicted +65 left 94 frames of stop at the flash end, as the engine said. Taken, 24 seeds: 22 deaths with the work charged to the decision, 19 with only gains of a horizon or more, 18 with free work, against 15.

The same preparation search with its choice switched off, work charged to the decision, 18 deaths; with its work free of the decision's budget, 14. The extra replays take work the stages after them need (the search for the next break runs through the flash on what is left), and a frame's work is what the game's 8 ms buys. Any search added to the flash frames is to be paid for outside the frame's work (a thread, or spread over frames), and each of the earlier lookahead results is to be read with that in mind: the first free-work measurement of a ranking key (with the free work) was 16.

Stop time bought by a chain does not carry the board: with the chain preparation chosen, flash ends with 60 or more frames of stop banked were fatal 10 of 391 (2.6%) against 1 of 473 (0.2%), and 28.1 panels at the flash end against 29.5. A chain spends panels (3 a link) and the board dies when the stop runs out with nothing to break.

Claim audit (each finder's claim against the engine's replay, 24 seeds x 12,000 frames, fixed budget): the search finder claimed a break on 17,625 lines and the engine confirmed 4,785 (27%), with its clock agreeing; the planner's main finder claimed 30,566 and 5,638 held (18%), 50% of its clocks 6+ frames late; on a 4,000-frame seed, 493 of its 495 claims were made while garbage was converting and moving, and failed. Not proposing them while a conversion runs was tried: 20 deaths against 15 (mean 7,046 against 8,332), so the failed claims are not waste: they are the lines that live and fill.

Planner clock: the planner priced a line at its walk and presses, but a pair under a converting block cannot be pressed until the block is gone; on a 4,000-frame seed every planner line of three swaps or more was 60 to 200+ frames later on the engine than priced. Priced with the board's own settle waits (as the search in time prices it): 300 of 303 lines now agree within 12 frames. Fixed-budget 24 seeds x 12,000 frames: seeds 25-48, 15 deaths and a mean of 10,082 against 15 and 8,332; seeds 1-24, 14 deaths and 7,774 against 15 and 7,837.

Of the lines the search in time finds and the engine judges, those it calls no use are almost all lines that would still be pressing when the board loses health (1,600 of 1,600 on a 5,000-frame seed): they finish inside the time the board has on paper and the pair they start on is not free until after it dies. They cost judge work, not survival.

Storage of the searches kept from frame to frame, four times the lines, steps and boards: fixed-budget seeds 1-8 at 30,000 frames, mean 11,619 frames against 9,624, none alive (the build before had seed 7 alive); think budget on the ordinary scan 0.19 frames over per 1,000 against the line of 1.0. The ready guide counting the three along the top row as well as the stacked one: on 2,500 recorded boards it separates boards a break is two swaps from from the rest slightly better (AUC 0.847 against 0.832). Fixed-budget scan of seeds 1-8: a mean of 9,733 frames against 11,619, none alive, eight seeds being too few to tell that apart from noise; kept, and tuned forward.

What a death is made of, 32 deaths of four ordinary scans read together: of the last landings, 25 had no break within 3 swaps on the board 2, 20 and 40 frames after it, and none had a board that 3 prep swaps (5 on 14 of them) at 150 frames before the landing could have made ready; the same holds for 90% of the landings that were survived, so a board that cannot be readied is the usual landing, not the fatal one.

The level-10 stack has 1 health, refilled only on a frame it is not topped out: a topped frame with no stop time and no lock is the death. Garbage does not drop while the stack is topped. Income of material is the break (6 panels a row); stop time and the lock of a match are the spend.

After a break converts a row the board offers a break within 3 swaps on 0 of 87 sampled boards, and a chain or a combo of four within 3 swaps on about half: the garbage above comes off mostly by the cascade the converted panels start, which the bot does not plan.

More search work a decision, fixed budget, seeds 1-8, mean frames: 1x 5,962; 2x 6,587; 4x 9,955; 8x 10,564 (one seed to 29,627). Each doubling moves the mean by under 2,000 and nothing reaches 30,000 at 8x: the limit is not search power.

Every death ends the same way: topped, stop time 0, the lock drops, health 0 one frame later. In the last 3,000 frames of each seed the board is locked 97-100% and stop time runs on 73-100% of frames, so a game is a chain of stop-time and pop windows that must overlap. The engine keeps the larger of the stop time running and the one awarded (checkMatches.awardStopTime), so an event started early wastes what remained. Garbage converts to panels from its own deterministic sequence (GeneratorSource.garbagePanelGenerator, seeded from the game seed), which the bot is not shown.

The gap after a pop (6ac305f..8fa1061, 508 gaps over four builds): a break pops for 38 + 7 x the garbage cells on screen (160-300 frames) and the stop time is frozen while it runs; between the pop's end and the next break's first match the gap has a median of 83 frames and a tail (25% over 147, 10% over 257), and 6.6% of gaps end in a death (stop banked at the pop's end: 0 12.5%, 1-39 7.8%, 40-79 6.4%, 80+ 2.9%). The gap is the swaps it takes: 6 in a median gap, 13 in gaps over 150, a one-swap break 24 frames; the break lines chosen run 5.7 swaps on average, 13.8 swaps a break all told.

What the swaps in a gap depend on: the converted row falls on each column's top, so a stack that is level when the pop ends leaves a flat row of six cells in six colours. Column height range 1: median gap 29 (12 gaps), 2: 51 (83), 3: 90 (265), 4: 94 (115), 5: 178 (32); 77% of pops end with a range of 3 or more. Pairs atop columns (a colour with two stacked completes with any panel of that colour the row lands on) average 0.65 a pop; offline on the logged boards a single swap adds a pair colour in 90% of pop starts (0.66 -> 1.66) and two swaps reach 2.19.

Why nothing built them: (1) setupTwos was off for any topped board, i.e. the whole pop; (2) the pair count read the converted row as the top and found no pair under it; (3) the stages before it (ruled 14.5k, break search 18k, lineup 11k) left 1.3-4.7k of 55k; (4) the lineup toward a break was played during the pop, for a stack the converted row was about to cover (34% of the swaps made in pops); (5) the arbiter's readiness rule asked 'a break in reach when the slab lands' of a board whose pile held the queue back, and every setup lost to the hold.
